name: L-theanine

card.summary: Tea amino acid used as a cheap calming, focus supplement; small studies show stress effects, regulators call evidence insufficient.
card.note: EFSA found insufficient evidence for sleep, stress and cognition claims.

quick.overview:
L-theanine is an amino acid from tea sold as a calming, focus-boosting supplement, often paired with caffeine.

Small studies report reduced stress responses, but EFSA and recent reviews describe evidence as limited.
quick.mechanism: Resembles glutamate and weakly interacts with glutamate receptors in lab studies.
quick.risks: Safety data are limited; a German agency warned about effects with sedatives. It is OTC in the US and GRAS up to 250 mg per serving in foods.

lead: L-theanine is a non-proteinogenic amino acid found mainly in tea leaves (Camellia sinensis) and sold as an over-the-counter supplement for relaxation, focus and sleep, often alongside caffeine.[1] It was identified in green tea in 1949 and isolated from gyokuro leaves in Kyoto in 1950.[1]

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a cheap, low-drama way to take the edge off coffee, calm anxiety, concentrate on studying and sleep better. Proponents link calmer stress responses and better sleep with how a person looks and presents: skin, eyes, mood and confidence.[13][14] The chain is indirect and is made by users rather than by studies of appearance.

Small human trials report reduced stress responses, effects on attention and mood when paired with caffeine, and some improvements in subjective sleep measures.[6][17][18][15] The European Food Safety Authority found in 2011 that evidence was insufficient to support claims for cognition, stress or sleep, and a 2025 review criticised the reliability of much of the literature, so the research is described as mixed.[1]
infobox: Tea leaves (about 1 to 2 percent of dry weight in green tea), supplements[1]
Capsules, tablets, powders, tea and some energy drinks
Onset about 1 hour; half-life roughly 0.8 to 1.2 hours[1]
OTC supplement; FDA GRAS in foods up to 250 mg per serving since 2007; approved for food use in Japan 1964[1]

sections.h: How it is used to look and feel better
paras: Looksmaxxing users take L-theanine mainly for three reasons. The first is to pair it with coffee or other caffeine so that alertness comes with less jitteriness; the second is to relax in the evening and fall asleep more easily; the third is to feel calmer and more focused while studying or working.[13][14] Forum posters say it calms without making them sleepy.[13]

The appearance reasoning is a chain: calmer stress responses and better sleep are said to support clearer skin, a rested face and steadier mood, and better focus supports training and study routines. Posts describing it as 'one of the best supplements' are about feeling and performance, not about direct changes to the face.[13] It is commonly stacked with other sleep and relaxation supplements; one thread discusses combining it with magnesium glycinate and GABA and reports sleeping very late into the day.[22]

Theanine makes up about 1 percent of the dry weight of black, green and white tea, and shaded teas such as matcha and gyokuro contain more.[1] It contributes to the umami taste of Japanese green tea.[4] Commercial products may contain some D-form because heat and pH can convert the natural L-form.[1]
Because green tea also contains caffeine, a cup of tea delivers both compounds in the same drink, which is one reason researchers study the combination.[1][19]

After oral intake it is absorbed in the small intestine and broken down to glutamate and ethylamine in the intestine and liver.[1] In laboratory work it binds glutamate receptors much more weakly than glutamate itself, blocks AMPA and kainate receptors, partially acts at NMDA receptors, and affects glutamate transporters.[1] A systematic review of caffeine and theanine describes theanine as behaving like a glutamate reuptake inhibitor and low-affinity glutamate receptor antagonist, with proposed action at GABA-A receptors.[20]
A small study found an EEG alpha-wave effect for GABA but compared it with theanine in the same experiment.[5]

A 2007 randomised trial in twelve volunteers found that L-theanine reduced psychological and physiological stress responses to a mental arithmetic task.[6] A 2020 systematic review of nine randomised trials of supplement-only theanine concluded that 200 to 400 mg per day may help reduce stress and anxiety in people exposed to stressful conditions, but called for longer and larger studies before it could be justified as a therapeutic agent.[16]

A 2019 randomised, placebo-controlled crossover trial of 30 adults found lower scores on a depression scale, trait anxiety and a sleep quality index after four weeks of 200 mg daily, with better verbal fluency and executive function scores.[17]

A 2008 study examined theanine, caffeine and the combination on cognition and mood.[7] Another 2008 trial in 27 volunteers compared 50 mg of caffeine with and without 100 mg of theanine: the combination improved speed and accuracy of attention-switching at 60 minutes and reduced susceptibility to distraction in a memory task, while caffeine alone raised subjective alertness.[18] A 2010 trial reported that the combination improved cognitive performance and increased subjective alertness.[19]

A 2021 systematic review of caffeine and theanine in the context of attention and ADHD covered the neurotransmitter mechanisms proposed and reviewed trials.[20] A 2021 randomised study examined theanine and cognitive function in middle-aged and older subjects.[21]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (19 articles, 897 participants, 18 in the meta-analysis) found that theanine improved subjective sleep onset latency, daytime dysfunction and overall subjective sleep quality, with small to moderate effect sizes; the authors noted a lack of studies of 'pure' theanine and called for more research.[15] The 2019 crossover trial found reduced scores on sleep latency, disturbance and sleep medication use subscales.[17]

Safety data are limited. In 2003 Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment objected to adding isolated theanine to drinks, warning of possible effects on psychomotor skills and on alcohol and sedatives.[1] In the US it is sold as a supplement and the FDA considers it generally recognised as safe in foods up to 250 mg per serving; Japan approved its food use in 1964.[1]
In November 2023 Slovenia banned sales of Prime energy drinks because theanine is not permitted in non-alcoholic beverages there.[1] A 2017 review covers its metabolism, health effects and safety.[8]

Registered studies include a phase 2 trial in boys with ADHD (n=100),[9] a trial of caffeine and theanine on cerebral blood flow, cognition and mood (n=24),[10] a phase 3 trial in schizophrenia (n=60),[11] and a study in trained athletes.[12] Published findings include the 2007 stress study,[6] the 2008 and 2010 caffeine combination trials,[7][18][19] a 2019 four-week trial,[17] and systematic reviews on stress, sleep and cognition.[15][16][20] In 2011 the EFSA found claims for cognition, stress and sleep unsupported, a 2024 review reported possible benefit over placebo for symptoms linked to anxiety disorders, ADHD and schizophrenia, and a 2025 review criticised unreliable trials.[1]

On looksmax.org it appears as an entry-level supplement. One poster calls it 'very cheap' and says it calms without sedation; a reply says it made them feel worse when taken in the morning, which they attribute to cortisol suppression, and the original poster says they take it later in the day.[13] A 2025 thread asks whether it helps focus while studying on low sleep, and a reply calls it benign.[14] Other threads mention it alongside coffee and aspirin before lifting, and a Hacker News discussion in 2024 covered a self-experiment with theanine on sleep and cognition.[23][24]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org it is described as a cheap, benign calming supplement used with caffeine.[13][14]

claims.believers: A poster calls it very cheap and effective, taken before bed or before a test, and says it calms without making you sleepy.[13]
claims.experts: A small 2007 study found reduced stress responses and a 2020 review of nine trials suggested possible benefit under stress, while EFSA found the claim unsupported.[6][16][1]

claims.claim: Combining it with caffeine improves focus.
claims.experts: Trials in 2008 and 2010 reported better attention-switching and alertness for the combination, while the EFSA did not accept cognition claims.[18][19][1]

claims.claim: It helps focus on low sleep.
claims.believers: A thread asks whether it improves study focus on low sleep, with one reply calling it benign.[14]
claims.experts: No studies found on this specific use.

claims.claim: It can backfire in the morning.
claims.believers: One user reports feeling bad taking it in the morning and attributes this to cortisol suppression.[13]
claims.experts: No studies found supporting a cortisol mechanism.

claims.claim: It helps you fall asleep and sleep better.
claims.believers: Posters take it before bed to relax and sleep, and one thread mixes it with magnesium and GABA.[13][22]
claims.experts: A 2025 meta-analysis of 19 articles found improved subjective sleep onset latency and quality, while noting few studies of pure theanine; EFSA found sleep claims unsupported in 2011.[15][1]

claims.claim: Theanine is a safe, mild supplement.
claims.believers: A forum reply calls it 'pretty benign'.[14]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports limited safety data, a German agency objection in 2003 and a Slovenian ban of a drink containing it in 2023, alongside FDA GRAS status up to 250 mg per serving in foods.[1]
